rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ النُّعْمَانُ بْنُ ثَابِتٍ
rows.notes: Bedrock legal pioneer of the Hanafi school. Prioritized robust legal frameworks, text-critical local transmissions of Kūfa, and Qiyās (legal analogy). His narrations are heavily evaluated by modern compilers; text-critical analyses underscore his extensive legal mastery and foundational role in preserving early Iraqi traditions (Āthār).
rows.works: Al-Fiqh al-Akbar, Kitāb al-Āthār (Transmitted via students), Musnad Abī Ḥanīfah
rows.quranWorks: No tafsir of his own survives; his rulings on āyāt come through his students
rows.authority: The Umayyad Caliphate, then the Abbasid Caliphate (al-Manṣūr)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ مَالِكُ بْنُ أَنَسٍ الْأَصْبَحِيُّ
rows.notes: Leader of the School of Madīnah (Imām Dār al-Hijrah). His Muwaṭṭaʾ represents the pinnacle of early transmission validity. Universally authenticated by classical and modern critics (including Al-Albani). Strongly prioritized and enforced the foundational rule: "Learn Adab (etiquette) before seeking knowledge."
rows.quranWorks: No tafsir; tafsir narrations inside al-Muwaṭṭaʾ
rows.authority: The Umayyad Caliphate, then the Abbasid Caliphate (al-Manṣūr, al-Mahdī, Hārūn al-Rashīd)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو يُوسُفَ يَعْقُوبُ بْنُ إِبْرَاهِيمَ الْأَنْصَارِيُّ
rows.study: Kūfa (under Abū Ḥanīfah & Ibn Abī Laylā)
rows.notes: First Chief Justice (Qāḍī al-Quḍāt) in Islamic history. Masterful Hadith memory. His specific recension of Kitāb al-Āthār preserves the earliest layer of Ḥanāfī transmissions, though it lacks a cover-to-cover modern English translation. Critically relied upon by early traditionists.
rows.works: Kitāb al-Āthār (Abū Yūsuf Recension), Al-Radd ʿalā Siyar al-Awzāʿī, Kitāb al-Kharāj
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate (chief judge under al-Mahdī, al-Hādī and Hārūn al-Rashīd)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ الْحَسَنِ الشَّيْبَانِيُّ
rows.notes: Great codifier of Ḥanāfī jurisprudence. His transmissions of Kitāb al-Āthār and his version of Al-Muwaṭṭaʾ are monumental. His recension of the Āthār has been fully translated into English by Turath Publishing. Highly accurate narrator bridging Iraqi and Hijazi systems.
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate (Hārūn al-Rashīd)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ إِدْرِيسَ الشَّافِعِيُّ
rows.notes: Architect of systematic legal theory (Uṣūl al-Fiqh) through his Epistle (Al-Risālah). Highly rigorous Hadith critic and completely trustworthy narrator. Modern scholarly English translations of his legal theory manuals are fully available (Lowry & Khadduri editions).
rows.quranWorks: Aḥkām al-Qurʾān, gathered from his works by al-Bayhaqī (d. 458)
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate (Hārūn al-Rashīd, al-Amīn, al-Maʾmūn)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ إِسْحَاقُ بْنُ رَاهَوَيْهِ الْمَرْوَزِيُّ
rows.notes: Revered as Amīr al-Mu'minīn fī al-Ḥadīth. Stellar teacher/mentor to Imāms al-Bukhārī, Muslim, at-Tirmidhmī, and an-Nasāʾī. His direct request inspired Bukhārī to compile his Sahīh. His massive Musnad was mostly lost; the surviving portion containing exactly 2,425 Hadiths is fully verified, printed, and digitally archived.
rows.quranWorks: His Tafsīr is lost; narrations survive in later books
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate; Khurasan under the Tahirids

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ حَنْبَلٍ الشَّيْبَانِيُّ
rows.notes: Founder of the Hanbali school and legendary traditionist. Collected over 27,000 Hadiths in his Musnad. Modern checking projects directed by contemporary giants (e.g., Sheikh Shu'ayb al-Arna'ut and Ahmad Shakir) meticulously graded and published every single chain across a monumental 50-volume set.
rows.works: Musnad Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, Kitāb al-Zuhd, Al-ʿIlal
rows.quranWorks: His Tafsīr is lost; his narrations on āyāt are in the Musnad
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate (al-Maʾmūn, al-Muʿtaṣim and al-Wāthiq, the Miḥnah; then al-Mutawakkil)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ إِسْمَاعِيلَ الْبُخَارِيُّ
rows.notes: The supreme master of Prophetic traditions. His Ṣaḥīḥ is held by unanimous Sunni consensus as the most authentic text after the Qur'ān. While his primary collection is universally canonical, his historical and ethical side-works (like Al-Adab al-Mufrad) are thoroughly evaluated and graded by modern authenticators like Al-Albani.
rows.works: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Al-Adab al-Mufrad, Al-Tārīkh al-Kabīr
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate; Khurasan and Transoxiana under the Tahirids and the Samanids

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ مُسْلِمُ بْنُ الْحَجَّاجِ الْقُشَيْرِيُّ
rows.notes: Celebrated pupil of Bukhārī and Ibn Rāhawayh. His Sahīh stands side-by-side with Bukhārī's in absolute authenticity, praised uniquely for its flawless thematic grouping of transmissions. Universally authenticated without reservation by classical and modern traditionists.
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate; Nīshāpūr under the Tahirids

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ ابْنُ مَاجَهْ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ يَزِيدَ الْقَزْوِينِيُّ
rows.notes: Compiler of the sixth canonical Sunan work. Highly valued for its thematic layout, though it contains a greater volume of weak (da'īf) and a few fabricated narrations than the other five. Meticulously parsed and divided into separate Sahīh and Da'īf volumes by Sheikh al-Albani.
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو دَاوُدَ سُلَيْمَانُ بْنُ الْأَشْعَثِ السِّجِسْتَانِيُّ
rows.notes: Foremost legal-tradition pupil of Imām Aḥmad. His Sunan maps legal rulings (Ahkām). Meticulously evaluated by modern science; Sheikh al-Albani spent years verifying its contents to separate the reliable traditions from the weak ones in his compiled Sahīh wa Da'īf Sunan Abī Dāwūd.
rows.quranWorks: Kitāb al-Ḥurūf wa al-Qirāʾāt, inside the Sunan
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو عِيسَى مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ عِيسَى التِّرْمِذِيُّ
rows.notes: Established the tripartite taxonomy of Hadith accuracy (Sahīh, Hasan, Da'īf) and comparative law annotations. Sheikh al-Albani critically cross-verified his entire text, dividing it into Sahīh and Da'īf categories, and authenticated his Shama'il.
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate; Transoxiana under the Tahirids, then the Samanids

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ شُعَيْبٍ النَّسَائِيُّ
rows.notes: Maintained exceptionally stringent narrator scrutiny metrics, second only to Bukhārī and Muslim. His Sunan al-Sughrā contains the lowest ratio of weak entries among the four classical Sunan texts. Fully analyzed and validated by modern verifiers into Sahīh and Da'īf indices.
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate; Egypt under the Tulunids, then Abbasid governors

rows.en: Imām Abū Jaʿfar Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī
rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ جَرِيرٍ الطَّبَرِيُّ
rows.study: Rayy, Baghdād, Basra, Kūfa, Egypt, Shām
rows.notes: The imām of the mufassirūn. His Jāmiʿ al-Bayān gathers the Companions' and Successors' narrations on every āyah with their chains, then weighs them and gives his own choice. The base book for Approaches 28–30.
rows.works: Jāmiʿ al-Bayān ʿan Taʾwīl Āy al-Qurʾān; Tārīkh al-Rusul wa al-Mulūk
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate (Baghdad)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ الطَّحَاوِيُّ
rows.notes: Titan of comparative legal jurisprudence and theological creed. His massive comparative text faded into manuscript obscurity but was structurally saved by al-Jassas's abridgement. His standard on creed (Al-ʿAqīdah al-Ṭaḥāwiyyah) is universally accepted; Sheikh al-Albani authored a definitive checking (Tahrīj) confirming its sound traditional metrics.
rows.works: Al-ʿAqīdah al-Ṭaḥāwiyyah, Sharḥ Maʿānī al-Āthār, Mukhtaṣar Ikhtilāf al-ʿUlamāʾ
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate; Egypt under the Tulunids, then Abbasid governors

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ عَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنُ أَبِي حَاتِمٍ الرَّازِيُّ
rows.study: Rayy, Iraq, Hijāz, Shām, Egypt (with his father Abū Ḥātim)
rows.notes: Hadith critic and son of Abū Ḥātim. His tafsir gives only narrations, each with its chain, from the Prophet ﷺ, the Companions and the Successors, with no opinions of his own.
rows.works: Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm (musnad); al-Jarḥ wa al-Taʿdīl
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate; Rayy under local amirs (Samanids and others)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو مَنْصُورٍ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ الْمَاتُرِيدِيُّ
rows.notes: Hanafi theologian of Samarqand; the Māturīdī creed is named after him. His Taʾwīlāt is among the earliest whole tafsirs written by one author.
rows.authority: The Samanids (Samarqand), under the Abbasid Caliphate

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو الْقَاسِمِ سُلَيْمَانُ بْنُ أَحْمَدَ الطَّبَرَانِيُّ
rows.notes: Compiled three massive encyclopedic Hadith dictionaries. Collected the specific narration instructing parents to teach children three things (Loving the Prophet, the Ahl al-Bayt, and the Qur'ān) under Hadith No. 861. Modern text-critical checks (Al-Albani, Al-Haythami) class this specific chain as Weak (Da'if) due to critics of the narrator Ja'far ibn Muhammad, though valid for moral training.
rows.works: Al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr (Hadith 861), Al-Muʿjam al-Awsat, Al-Muʿjam al-Ṣaghīr
rows.quranWorks: Tafsir narrations inside his three Muʿjams
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate; Isfahan under the Buyids

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو بَكْرٍ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ عَلِيٍّ الْجَصَّاصُ
rows.notes: Eminent Ḥanāfī master jurist. His structural abridgement of Imām al-Ṭaḥāwī’s massive comparative manual saved the text from complete historical loss. His Ahkām al-Qurʾān stands as the premier exegesis text for legal derivation in the Ḥanāfī school.
rows.works: Ahkām al-Qurʾān, Sharḥ Mukhtaṣar al-Ṭaḥāwī, Abridgement of Ikhtilāf al-ʿUlamāʾ
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate under the Buyids (Baghdad)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو اللَّيْثِ نَصْرُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ السَّمَرْقَنْدِيُّ
rows.notes: Hanafi faqih and preacher, called Imām al-Hudā. His tafsir Baḥr al-ʿUlūm joins narrations with plain explanation.
rows.authority: The Samanids (Samarqand)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو إِسْحَاقَ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ الثَّعْلَبِيُّ
rows.notes: Master of al-Wāḥidī. A very large tafsir that gathers earlier books; it carries many weak narrations and Isrāʾīliyyāt, so each one needs checking.
rows.works: al-Kashf wa al-Bayān ʿan Tafsīr al-Qurʾān
rows.authority: The Ghaznavids (Nīshāpūr), under the Abbasid Caliphate

rows.en: Imām Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib al-Qaysī
rows.ar: الإِمَامُ مَكِّيُّ بْنُ أَبِي طَالِبٍ الْقَيْسِيُّ
rows.notes: Andalusian master of the Qirāʾāt and of the grammar of the Qurʾān. His al-Hidāyah is a large tafsir of the Maliki West.
rows.works: al-Hidāyah ilā Bulūgh al-Nihāyah; al-Kashf ʿan Wujūh al-Qirāʾāt
rows.authority: The Umayyad Caliphate of Cordoba, then the Taifa kingdoms

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ عَلِيُّ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ الْمَاوَرْدِيُّ
rows.notes: Shafiʿi jurist and chief judge. His tafsir lists the different readings of each āyah side by side, which suits comparing views.
rows.works: al-Nukat wa al-ʿUyūn; al-Aḥkām al-Sulṭāniyyah; al-Ḥāwī al-Kabīr
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate (al-Qādir, al-Qāʾim) under the Buyids, then the Seljuks

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو بَكْرٍ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ الْحُسَيْنِ الْبَيْهَقِيُّ
rows.notes: Great Shafiʿi traditionist. He gathered al-Shāfiʿī's own words on the āyāt of rulings into one book.
rows.works: Aḥkām al-Qurʾān lil-Shāfiʿī (gathered); al-Sunan al-Kubrā; Shuʿab al-Īmān
rows.authority: The Ghaznavids, then the Seljuks

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو الْقَاسِمِ عَبْدُ الْكَرِيمِ بْنُ هَوَازِنَ الْقُشَيْرِيُّ
rows.notes: Shafiʿi, Ashʿari and Sufi. His tafsir gives the Sufi 'indications' (ishārāt) of the āyāt, so it belongs with the groups (36), named as Sufi.
rows.source: Check (one per-āyah file is mislabelled) · free (classical)
rows.authority: The Ghaznavids, then the Seljuks

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ عَلِيُّ بْنُ أَحْمَدَ الْوَاحِدِيُّ
rows.notes: Student of al-Thaʿlabī. Wrote three tafsirs (long, middle, short) and the best-known book on the reasons for revelation (Asbāb al-Nuzūl).
rows.source: Open per āyah (spot-check: the file for 2:1 holds another book's text) · free (classical)
rows.authority: The Ghaznavids, then the Seljuks

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو الْمُظَفَّرِ مَنْصُورُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ السَّمْعَانِيُّ
rows.notes: Hanafi who became Shafiʿi; a scholar of uṣūl. A clear, moderate tafsir, close to the early narrations.
rows.authority: The Seljuks (Merv)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ الْحُسَيْنُ بْنُ مَسْعُودٍ الْبَغَوِيُّ
rows.birth: Bagh, between Herat and Marw al-Rūdh (c. 436 AH)
rows.notes: Called Muḥyī al-Sunnah. His tafsir is a careful, shorter work drawn from al-Thaʿlabī, keeping the narrations and leaving out much that is weak.
rows.works: Maʿālim al-Tanzīl; Sharḥ al-Sunnah; Maṣābīḥ al-Sunnah
rows.authority: The Seljuks (Sultan Sanjar)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو الْقَاسِمِ مَحْمُودُ بْنُ عُمَرَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ
rows.study: Bukhārā, Baghdād, Makkah (lived there: Jār Allāh)
rows.notes: Master of Arabic rhetoric (balāghah). His tafsir is unmatched on language, and Muʿtazili in creed, so it is read as a group's view (36), with later Sunni notes on it.
rows.madhab: Hanafi in fiqh · Muʿtazili in creed
rows.authority: The Seljuks and the Khwarazm-shahs; Makkah under its Sharifs

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ عَبْدُ الْحَقِّ بْنُ غَالِبِ بْنِ عَطِيَّةَ
rows.notes: Maliki judge of al-Andalus. A careful tafsir on language and narrations; al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān drew much from it.
rows.works: al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz fī Tafsīr al-Kitāb al-ʿAzīz
rows.authority: The Almoravids (al-Andalus)

rows.en: Qāḍī Abū Bakr Ibn al-ʿArabī al-Maʿāfirī
rows.ar: الْقَاضِي أَبُو بَكْرٍ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللهِ ابْنُ الْعَرَبِيِّ
rows.notes: Maliki judge. His Aḥkām al-Qurʾān is the Maliki book on the āyāt of rulings. (Not the Sufi Ibn ʿArabī, d. 638.)
rows.works: Aḥkām al-Qurʾān; ʿĀriḍat al-Aḥwadhī; al-ʿAwāṣim min al-Qawāṣim
rows.authority: The Almoravids, then the Almohads

rows.ar: الْفَضْلُ بْنُ الْحَسَنِ الطَّبْرِسِيُّ
rows.notes: The main classical Shiʿi (Imāmī) tafsir. Read as a group's view (36), named as Shiʿi, never mixed with the madhabs.
rows.authority: The Seljuks (Khurasan, Sultan Sanjar)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو الْفَرَجِ عَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنُ عَلِيٍّ ابْنُ الْجَوْزِيِّ
rows.notes: Hanbali preacher and scholar. Zād al-Masīr lists the different sayings on each āyah briefly, with who said them.
rows.works: Zād al-Masīr fī ʿIlm al-Tafsīr; Talbīs Iblīs; Nuzhat al-Aʿyun
rows.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate (al-Mustanjid, al-Mustaḍīʾ, al-Nāṣir), after the Seljuks declined

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ فَخْرُ الدِّينِ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ عُمَرَ الرَّازِيُّ
rows.notes: Shafiʿi and Ashʿari theologian. His great tafsir argues each āyah's meaning with reason and answers the sects of his time.
rows.authority: The Khwarazm-shahs and the Ghurids (Herat)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ عِزُّ الدِّينِ عَبْدُ الْعَزِيزِ بْنُ عَبْدِ السَّلَامِ
rows.notes: Called Sulṭān al-ʿUlamāʾ; he spoke openly against rulers. Wrote a short tafsir abridged from al-Māwardī.
rows.authority: The Ayyubids (Damascus), then the Mamluk Sultanate (Cairo)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو عَبْدِ اللهِ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ أَحْمَدَ الْقُرْطُبِيُّ
rows.notes: Maliki. His tafsir gathers the rulings of each āyah with the views of all the madhabs; the first book for an āyah of rulings (for example 2:228).
rows.authority: The Almohads (Cordoba), then the Ayyubids and Mamluks (Egypt)

rows.ar: الْقَاضِي نَاصِرُ الدِّينِ عَبْدُ اللهِ بْنُ عُمَرَ الْبَيْضَاوِيُّ
rows.notes: Shafiʿi and Ashʿari. A short, dense tafsir (largely from al-Kashshāf without its Muʿtazili views) that became the teaching text of the madrasahs, with many glosses.
rows.authority: The Salghurids of Fars, then the Ilkhanids

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو الْبَرَكَاتِ عَبْدُ اللهِ بْنُ أَحْمَدَ النَّسَفِيُّ
rows.notes: Hanafi and Māturīdī. A short, clear tafsir, much used in Hanafi lands.
rows.works: Madārik al-Tanzīl wa Ḥaqāʾiq al-Taʾwīl; Kanz al-Daqāʾiq
rows.authority: The Ilkhanids

rows.ar: شَيْخُ الْإِسْلَامِ تَقِيُّ الدِّينِ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الْحَلِيمِ ابْنُ تَيْمِيَّةَ
rows.death: Damascus, in prison at the citadel (728 AH)
rows.notes: Hanbali. Wrote no complete tafsir, but much on the method of tafsir and on single sūrahs and āyāt; gathered later from his fatwas.
rows.works: Muqaddimah fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr; tafsir parts of Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā
rows.quranWorks: Muqaddimah fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr; Daqāʾiq al-Tafsīr (gathered)
rows.authority: The Mamluk Sultanate

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ عَلَاءُ الدِّينِ عَلِيُّ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ الْخَازِنُ
rows.notes: Shafiʿi. His tafsir is drawn mostly from al-Baghawī, with stories added.
rows.authority: The Mamluk Sultanate

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو الْقَاسِمِ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ أَحْمَدَ ابْنُ جُزَيٍّ الْكَلْبِيُّ
rows.notes: Maliki scholar of Granada who died fighting. A short tafsir with a valuable introduction on the sciences of the Qurʾān.
rows.authority: The Nasrids of Granada

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو حَيَّانَ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ يُوسُفَ الْأَنْدَلُسِيُّ
rows.notes: The great grammarian. His tafsir is the fullest on the grammar and readings of each āyah.
rows.authority: The Nasrids (Granada), then the Mamluk Sultanate (Cairo)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ شَمْسُ الدِّينِ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ أَبِي بَكْرٍ ابْنُ قَيِّمِ الْجَوْزِيَّةِ
rows.notes: Hanbali, student of Ibn Taymiyyah. No complete tafsir, but long passages on āyāt across his books, gathered later.
rows.works: al-Tafsīr al-Qayyim / Badāʾiʿ al-Tafsīr (gathered); Zād al-Maʿād; Iʿlām al-Muwaqqiʿīn
rows.authority: The Mamluk Sultanate

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ عِمَادُ الدِّينِ إِسْمَاعِيلُ بْنُ عُمَرَ ابْنُ كَثِيرٍ
rows.notes: Shafiʿi traditionist and historian. Explains the Qurʾān by the Qurʾān, then the Sunnah, then the Companions, with chains; the most read tafsir today.
rows.works: Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm; al-Bidāyah wa al-Nihāyah
rows.authority: The Mamluk Sultanate

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ جَلَالُ الدِّينِ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ أَحْمَدَ الْمَحَلِّيُّ
rows.notes: Shafiʿi. Wrote the first half of Tafsīr al-Jalālayn (al-Kahf to the end, and al-Fātiḥah); al-Suyūṭī finished it.
rows.works: Tafsīr al-Jalālayn (with al-Suyūṭī); Sharḥ Jamʿ al-Jawāmiʿ
rows.authority: The Mamluk Sultanate

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ عَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ الثَّعَالِبِيُّ
rows.notes: Maliki of North Africa. A tafsir that summarises Ibn ʿAṭiyyah with other sources.
rows.authority: The Zayyanids and the Hafsids (Algiers changed hands)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ أَبُو حَفْصٍ عُمَرُ بْنُ عَلِيٍّ ابْنُ عَادِلٍ
rows.notes: Hanbali. A very large tafsir on the language, readings and rulings of each āyah. Dates are uncertain.
rows.authority: The Mamluk Sultanate

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ بُرْهَانُ الدِّينِ إِبْرَاهِيمُ بْنُ عُمَرَ الْبِقَاعِيُّ
rows.notes: Shafiʿi. His tafsir is on the order and links between āyāt and sūrahs (munāsabāt), which suits Approach 'its passage'.
rows.works: Naẓm al-Durar fī Tanāsub al-Āyāt wa al-Suwar
rows.authority: The Mamluk Sultanate

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ جَلَالُ الدِّينِ عَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنُ أَبِي بَكْرٍ السُّيُوطِيُّ
rows.notes: Shafiʿi; wrote on every science. al-Durr al-Manthūr gathers the narrations on each āyah (useful for 28 and 29, with grades to check); he finished al-Jalālayn.
rows.works: al-Durr al-Manthūr; Tafsīr al-Jalālayn (al-Baqarah to al-Isrāʾ); al-Itqān; Lubāb al-Nuqūl
rows.source: Jalālayn open per āyah; al-Durr OpenITI · free (classical)
rows.authority: The Mamluk Sultanate (he died in 911 AH, before the Uthmanis took Egypt)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ عَلَاءُ الدِّينِ عَلِيُّ بْنُ حِسَامِ الدِّينِ الْمُتَّقِي الْهِنْدِيُّ
rows.notes: Masterful Hadith aggregator. Systematically re-arranged thousands of traditions into his encyclopedia Kanz al-Ummal. Preserved al-Tabarani's "three qualities character training" Hadith as Entry No. 45467. Modern verifiers examine the source texts inside his compilation to evaluate individual transmission lines.
rows.works: Kanz al-ʿUmmāl fī Sunan al-Aqvāl wa-al-Afʿāl (Hadith 45467)
rows.quranWorks: Kanz al-ʿUmmāl has a chapter of tafsir narrations
rows.authority: The Sultanate of Gujarat, then Makkah under the Mamluks and the Uthmani Khilafah

rows.ar: شَيْخُ الْإِسْلَامِ أَبُو السُّعُودِ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ الْعِمَادِيُّ
rows.lived: Istanbul (Shaykh al-Islām of the Uthmani state)
rows.notes: Hanafi; the chief scholar of the Uthmani state under Sulaymān. A tafsir on the eloquence of the āyāt; an example of a scholar under the Khilafah's authority.
rows.works: Irshād al-ʿAql al-Salīm ilā Mazāyā al-Kitāb al-Karīm
rows.authority: The Uthmani Khilafah (Sulaymān I, Selim II)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ زَيْنُ الدِّينِ مُحَمَّدٌ عَبْدُ الرَّؤُوفِ الْمُنَاوِيُّ
rows.notes: Foremost commentator of the late classical era. In his commentary Fayd al-Qadir (Vol 1, Page 225), he meticulously evaluated the "teach your children three things" Hadith, explicitly noting its transmission weaknesses while confirming its sound text for ethical cultivation.
rows.quranWorks: None on the Qurʾān (his works are on Hadith)
rows.authority: The Uthmani Khilafah (Egypt)

rows.ar: شِهَابُ الدِّينِ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ الْخَفَاجِيُّ
rows.notes: Hanafi. His gloss on al-Bayḍāwī is the largest of its kind.
rows.works: ʿInāyat al-Qāḍī wa Kifāyat al-Rāḍī (gloss on al-Bayḍāwī)
rows.authority: The Uthmani Khilafah

rows.ar: إِسْمَاعِيلُ حَقِّي الْبُرُوسَوِيُّ
rows.notes: Uthmani Hanafi and Sufi (Jalwatī order). A long tafsir full of Sufi counsel; read as a Sufi view (36).
rows.authority: The Uthmani Khilafah

rows.ar: الشَّاهُ وَلِيُّ اللهِ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الرَّحِيمِ الدِّهْلَوِيُّ
rows.notes: Reviver of Hadith study in India; translated the Qurʾān into Persian and wrote on the principles of tafsir. A root of the scholarship of the Indian subcontinent.
rows.works: al-Fawz al-Kabīr fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr; Fatḥ al-Raḥmān (Persian translation); Ḥujjat Allāh al-Bālighah
rows.authority: The Mughals, in their decline; the Durrani and Maratha wars

rows.ar: الشَّيْخُ سُلَيْمَانُ بْنُ عُمَرَ الْجَمَلُ
rows.notes: Shafiʿi of al-Azhar. His gloss on al-Jalālayn is the fullest.
rows.authority: The Uthmani Khilafah (Egypt under its Mamluk beys)

rows.ar: الشَّاهُ عَبْدُ الْعَزِيزِ الدِّهْلَوِيُّ
rows.study: Delhi (under his father, Shāh Walī Allāh)
rows.notes: Son of Shāh Walī Allāh. His Persian tafsir was given under British rule in India.
rows.authority: The late Mughals; the British East India Company (Delhi from 1218 AH)

rows.ar: الشَّيْخُ أَحْمَدُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ الصَّاوِيُّ
rows.notes: Maliki and Sufi (Khalwatī). A gloss on al-Jalālayn, much read in Egypt and West Africa.
rows.authority: The Uthmani Khilafah; Egypt under Muhammad ʿAlī (from 1220 AH)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ عَلِيٍّ الشَّوْكَانِيُّ
rows.notes: Born a Zaydi; became an independent mujtahid who called for leaving blind following. Fatḥ al-Qadīr joins narration and reasoning.
rows.authority: The Zaydi Imams of Yemen (Qāsimī state)

rows.ar: الإِمَامُ شِهَابُ الدِّينِ مَحْمُودُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللهِ الْآلُوسِيُّ
rows.notes: Hanafi mufti of Baghdād under the late Uthmani state. A large tafsir that gathers the earlier books, on language, rulings and Sufi meanings.
rows.authority: The Uthmani Khilafah (Baghdad)

rows.ar: الشَّيْخُ جَمَالُ الدِّينِ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ الْقَاسِمِيُّ
rows.notes: Reformer of Damascus. His tafsir quotes the earlier scholars at length.
rows.authority: The Uthmani Khilafah (Damascus)

rows.ar: الشَّيْخُ مُحَمَّدُ رَشِيدُ رِضَا
rows.notes: Reformer, editor of al-Manār. His tafsir, begun from Muḥammad ʿAbduh's lessons, reads the āyāt against the condition of the Ummah after the Khilafah; it stops at 12:101.
rows.authority: Egypt under British occupation (from 1299 AH), then the Kingdom of Egypt

rows.ar: الشَّيْخُ أَحْمَدُ مُصْطَفَى الْمَرَاغِيُّ
rows.notes: A complete tafsir in plain modern Arabic, following al-Manār's method.
rows.authority: Egypt under British occupation, then the Kingdom of Egypt

rows.ar: الشَّيْخُ عَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنُ نَاصِرٍ السَّعْدِيُّ
rows.notes: Hanbali. A short, clear tafsir on the guidance and lessons of each āyah; good for students.
rows.authority: Najd under Ibn Rashīd, then the Saudi state (the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia from 1351 AH)

rows.ar: الشَّيْخُ مُحَمَّدٌ الْأَمِينُ الشِّنْقِيطِيُّ
rows.notes: Maliki. His tafsir explains the Qurʾān by the Qurʾān, with long discussions of rulings.
rows.works: Aḍwāʾ al-Bayān fī Īḍāḥ al-Qurʾān bil-Qurʾān
rows.authority: French colonial Mauritania, then the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia

rows.ar: الشَّيْخُ مُحَمَّدٌ الطَّاهِرُ ابْنُ عَاشُورٍ
rows.notes: Maliki; master of the aims of the Sharīʿah (maqāṣid). A large tafsir on language, eloquence and purpose.
rows.works: al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr; Maqāṣid al-Sharīʿah al-Islāmiyyah
rows.authority: The French Protectorate of Tunisia (Husaynid beys), then the Republic of Tunisia

rows.ar: الشَّيْخُ مُحَمَّدُ نَاصِرُ الدِّينِ الْأَلْبَانِيُّ
rows.lived: Syria, Jordan, Saudi Arabia (Univ. of Madīnah)
rows.notes: The most influential modern Sunni Hadith verifier. Pioneered systematic digital-era Takhrij (chain analysis). Divided the classical Sunan works into independent Sahīh and Da'īf indices. Evaluated the "teach your children three things" tradition and declared it Weak (Da'if) in Da'īf al-Jāmiʿ, No. 2634.
rows.works: Silsilat al-Aḥādīth al-Ṣaḥīḥah, Silsilat al-Aḥādīth al-Ḍaʿīfah, Irwāʾ al-Ghalīl, Ṣaḥīḥ wa Ḍaʿīf al-Jāmiʿ
rows.quranWorks: None on the Qurʾān; his grades are shown beside narrations
rows.authority: The French Mandate, then the Syrian Republic; Saudi Arabia; Jordan

rows.ar: الشَّيْخُ شُعَيْبُ بْنُ مُحَاوَرَ الْأَرْنَاوُوطُ
rows.notes: Monumental modern Albanian-Syrian critical editor and manuscript investigator. Led the encyclopedic 50-volume critical authentication of Imām Aḥmad's Musnad, verifying thousands of narrators. Extensively checked early Hanafi-tradition compilations (such as al-Tahawi's texts).
rows.works: Tahqīq of Musnad Aḥmad (50 Vols), Tahqīq of Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, Tahqīq of Sharḥ Maʿānī al-Āthār
rows.quranWorks: None on the Qurʾān; his grades are shown beside narrations
rows.authority: The French Mandate, then the Syrian Republic; Jordan

2.authority: The Umayyad Caliphate (Damascus) to 132 AH, then the Abbasid Caliphate (Baghdad from 145 AH); in al-Andalus the Umayyad Emirate of Cordoba (from 138 AH)

3.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate (Baghdad and Samarra), with local dynasties under it: the Tahirids and Saffarids (Khurasan), the Samanids (Transoxiana), the Tulunids (Egypt, 254–292 AH), the Aghlabids (Ifriqiya); in al-Andalus the Umayyad Emirate of Cordoba

4.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate, under Buyid control from 334 AH; the Samanids (Khurasan and Transoxiana); the Ikhshidids, then the Fatimids (Egypt, from 358 AH); the Hamdanids (Aleppo, Mosul); the Umayyad Caliphate of Cordoba (from 316 AH)

5.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate, under the Buyids and then the Seljuks (Baghdad, from 447 AH); the Ghaznavids (Khurasan, India); the Fatimids (Egypt); the Taifa kingdoms, then the Almoravids (al-Andalus, Maghrib)

6.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate with the Seljuks (Sultan Sanjar in Khurasan); the Khwarazm-shahs; the Zengids, then the Ayyubids (Egypt and Syria, from 567 AH); the Almoravids, then the Almohads (Maghrib, al-Andalus)

7.authority: The Abbasid Caliphate until the Mongols took Baghdad (656 AH); the Ayyubids, then the Mamluk Sultanate (Egypt and Syria, from 648 AH); the Ilkhanids (Iran, Iraq); the Delhi Sultanate; the Nasrids (Granada), the Hafsids, the Marinids

8.authority: The Mamluk Sultanate (Egypt, Syria, Hijaz; Abbasid caliphs in name only, in Cairo); the Ilkhanids and their successors (Iran); the Delhi Sultanate; the early Uthmani state (Anatolia); the Nasrids (Granada), the Marinids, the Hafsids

9.authority: The Mamluk Sultanate; the Timurids (Iran, Central Asia); the Uthmani state (Constantinople from 857 AH); the Hafsids and Zayyanids (North Africa); the Nasrids (Granada)

10.authority: The Uthmani Khilafah (Egypt, Syria and the Hijaz from 922–923 AH); the Safavids (Iran, from 907 AH); the Mughals (India, from 932 AH); the Saʿdians (Morocco)

11.authority: The Uthmani Khilafah; the Safavids (Iran); the Mughals (India); the Alawite sultans (Morocco, from 1075 AH)

12.authority: The Uthmani Khilafah; the Mughals, declining after 1118 AH; the Safavids, then the Afsharids and Zands (Iran); the Durranis (Afghanistan)

13.authority: The Uthmani Khilafah; Muhammad ʿAlī's dynasty in Egypt (from 1220 AH); the British East India Company in India (Delhi from 1218 AH); the Qajars (Iran); the Zaydi Imams (Yemen); the first and second Saudi states (Najd)

14.authority: The end of the Uthmani Khilafah (abolished 1342 AH / 1924 CE); British and French colonial rule and mandates; then new nation states (Egypt, Syria, Jordan, Saudi Arabia from 1351 AH, Pakistan, Tunisia …)

15.authority: Nation states across the Muslim world
